title: Gotama

teacherSummary.text: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and Siddhartha leaves, feeling Gotama has taken his friend but given him himself.

vocabulary.definition: One who is new in any business, profession, or calling
vocabulary.context: Then Govinda broke loose, embraced once again his childhood friend and left with the novices.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “novice”: nov (Latin novus, "new"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: (Card Playing) To throw out of one's hand, as superfluous cards
vocabulary.context: There is nothing to opinions, they may be beautiful or ugly, smart or foolish, everyone can support them or discard them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “discard”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To draw on, by exciting hope or desire
vocabulary.context: No teachings will entice me any more, since this man’s teachings have not enticed me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “entice”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “venerate”: ven (Latin venire, "to come") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: But attentively he looked at Gotama’s head, his shoulders, his feet, his quietly dangling hand, and it seemed to him as if every joint of every finger of this hand was of these teachings, spoke of, breathed of, exhaled the fragrant of, glistened of truth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “exhale”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: But attentively he looked at Gotama’s head, his shoulders, his feet, his quietly dangling hand, and it seemed to him as if every joint of every finger of this hand was of these teachings, spoke of, breathed of, exhaled the fragrant of, glistened of truth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “glisten”: ten (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being open
vocabulary.context: With half of a smile, with an unwavering openness and kindness, Gotama looked into the stranger’s eyes and bid him to leave with a hardly noticeable gesture.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “openness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The Buddha’s eyes quietly looked to the ground; quietly, in perfect equanimity his inscrutable face was smiling.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “equanimity”: anim (Latin anima, "breath, soul") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To hang loosely, or with a swinging or jerking motion
vocabulary.context: But attentively he looked at Gotama’s head, his shoulders, his feet, his quietly dangling hand, and it seemed to him as if every joint of every finger of this hand was of these teachings, spoke of, breathed of, exhaled the fragrant of, glistened of truth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dangle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: You have renounced your home and your parents, renounced your birth and possessions, renounced your free will, renounced all friendship.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “renounce”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Gotama is Siddhartha Gautama, the historical Buddha; Hesse deliberately gives his hero the Buddha's own name.

significance: The parting of friends dramatizes the novel's thesis that wisdom must be lived, not adopted.
discussionQuestions: Why does Siddhartha refuse to follow even a teacher he admires?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the unity of all things?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Gotama,” how does Hesse show the teacher and the teaching? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Gotama, how does Hesse develop the idea of the teacher and the teaching? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Gotama develops the idea of the teacher and the teaching. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Gotama (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the teacher and the teaching. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Gotama suggests about the teacher and the teaching. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses characterization in Gotama to complicate the reader's understanding of the teacher and the teaching. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Gotama within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the teacher and the teaching responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Gotama alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the teacher and the teaching follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Gotama and its treatment of the teacher and the teaching. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Gotama as evidence for a larger claim about the teacher and the teaching in Siddhartha. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Gotama as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the teacher and the teaching. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

options: To draw on, by exciting hope or desire
To hang loosely, or with a swinging or jerking motion

satQuestions.passage: The Buddha went on his way, modestly and deep in his thoughts, his calm face was neither happy nor sad, it seemed to smile quietly and inwardly. With a hidden smile, quiet, calm, somewhat resembling a healthy child, the Buddha walked, wore the robe and placed his feet just as all of his monks did, according to a precise rule. But his face and his walk, his quietly lowered glance, his quietly dangling hand and even every finger of his quietly dangling hand expressed peace, expressed perfection, did not search, did not imitate, breathed softly in an unwithering calm, in an unwithering light, an untouchable peace.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Gotama”?
options: Rejection and the turn to revenge

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Siddhartha refuse to follow even a teacher he admires? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are novices, discard, enticed, venerated, exhaled. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Then Govinda broke loose, embraced once again his childhood friend and left with the novices.” Webster's says: One who is new in any business, profession, or calling. Now the word history: “novice”: nov (Latin novus, "new"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “discard”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “entice”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Gotama is Siddhartha Gautama, the historical Buddha; Hesse deliberately gives his hero the Buddha's own name. Why does this chapter matter? The parting of friends dramatizes the novel's thesis that wisdom must be lived, not adopted. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the teacher and the teaching.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Conflict.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

But his face and his walk, his quietly lowered glance, his quietly dangling hand and even every finger of his quietly dangling hand expressed peace, expressed perfection, did not search, did not imitate, breathed softly in an unwithering calm, in an unwithering light, an untouchable peace.

segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Conflict: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Gotama,” how does Hesse show the teacher and the teaching? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the teacher and the teaching, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes the teacher and the teaching. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
